text: EU-OSHA defines heat stress as the overall heat load from metabolic heat, clothing and the environment: air temperature and movement, humidity and radiant heat.

text: Mild or moderate heat stress can cause discomfort and affect performance and safety without harming health; extremes compromise the body's ability to regulate its temperature.

text: Radiant heat reaches the body from hot objects such as hot metal, furnaces and steam pipes without contact; the sun is a common source.

text: Indoor workers are also at risk of heat stress, especially in poorly cooled buildings.

text: EU-OSHA's engineering controls include reducing heat release, reflective or heat-absorbing shielding, insulating or enclosing heat-generating processes or separating them from workers, and covering hot surfaces with low-emissivity material.
It lists reducing humidity by eliminating open hot water baths, drains and leaky steam valves, and removing heated air or steam from hot processes with local exhaust ventilation.
missing: euosha: "removing heated air or steam from hot processes using local exhaust ventilation"
euosha-pdf: "removing heated air or steam from hot processes using local exhaust ventilation"

text: It lists shading workers from direct sunlight with blinds or reflective film on windows, and positioning workstations away from direct sunlight or sources of heat.
missing: euosha: "positioning workstations away from direct sunlight"
euosha-pdf: "positioning workstations away from direct sunlight"

text: It lists fans and air movement, particularly in humid conditions, without compromising local exhaust ventilation installed on machinery.
It lists air-conditioned, shaded or cool break areas as close as possible to the work site.

text: In very hot industrial areas, ventilation, localised air conditioning and cooled observation booths are commonly used to provide cool workstations.
The risk assessment needs revising regularly and when conditions change, and technical or organisational changes need checking so that they do not increase the risk for workers.

text: EU-OSHA notes that the risk assessment already covers pregnant workers and may be reviewed when a worker says she is pregnant; in very hot work a pregnant woman's core temperature may rise.
On average about one litre of water an hour may be needed to replace sweat losses, and drinking every 15 to 20 minutes is encouraged: an average from guidance, not an individual prescription.

text: In the EU, the Workplaces Directive requires the temperature in rooms containing workstations to be adequate for human beings; most legislation sets no specific maximum, so national legislation needs checking.
